title: The Impact of Structured Cybersecurity Training on Behavioural Risk in Higher Education
content: This study examines whether structured cybersecurity training meaningfully reduces behavioural risk in higher education institutions, addressing persistent gaps between awareness and secure practice identified in prior socio-technical research. Using an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design, the research integrates deep learning-based predictive modelling of behavioural risk scores (n = 250) with qualitative thematic analysis of institutional interviews. Survey constructs captured training exposure, policy knowledge, best-practice adherence, risk tolerance, technical readiness, and perceived cybersecurity culture. A multi-layer neural network model was developed and validated through cross-validation procedures to estimate behavioural risk, followed by regression, mediation, and moderation analyses. Results indicate that participants receiving structured interactive training exhibited substantially lower predicted behavioural risk than untrained or awareness-only groups, with training intensity demonstrating a significant dose–response effect. Hierarchical regression shows that training predicts behavioural risk beyond policy knowledge and cognitive factors, while mediation analysis confirms partial knowledge-based pathways. Moderation analysis reveals that cybersecurity culture amplifies training effectiveness. Qualitative findings corroborate statistical results, highlighting structural training deficiencies and cultural marginalisation as key governance weaknesses. The study concludes that structured, culturally embedded training functions as a central behavioural determinant, and that predictive analytics can support evidence-based cybersecurity governance in higher education.
